extracted.intended_audience: Academic researchers preparing a resubmission/response to grant reviews (particularly NIH-style applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for interpreting a grant summary statement, writing the one-page introduction/response to reviewers, and making substantive revisions for an NIH-style resubmission (or new submission to other funders). Emphasizes tone, prioritization, documenting changes, and deciding whether to revise, reconceptualize, or abandon a project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deconstruct the summary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Go through the summary statement and pull out the comments enumerating them point by point; start to put them into thematic groups because some reviewers will have similar kinds of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at strengths as well as weaknesses; group similar comments across reviewers; use thematic grouping to identify major, recurring issues; consider cutting aims that all reviewers disliked and keep aims that resonated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get outside opinion on interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain another experienced reader to confirm you are reading the reviews correctly and to help decipher what reviewers are really saying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have someone experienced with summary statements read the critiques to ensure your interpretation matches others’; there is an art to deciphering reviewer intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your program officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult your program officer because they likely attended the discussion and may have notes or insight into why the score/critique mismatch occurred or what happened at the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers can provide frontline interpretation (especially after recent policy changes); for nondiscussed applications their ability to help is limited but still useful; you may have to talk to them to decide strategy (resubmit vs. new submission vs. other agency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a clear plan of attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop two tasks for resubmission: (1) write the one-page introduction/response and (2) make substantive changes in the proposal where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize major issues that drove the score; set timelines; do internal reviews and obtain feedback; treat the revision process with the same rigor as the original submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-page introduction — open with thanks and strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the response with a brief thank-you to reviewers and (optionally) a succinct enumeration of reviewer-noted strengths to open on a positive note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some debate exists about using space to list strengths, but include them succinctly because new reviewers may not have seen the original; begin with retained strengths and a statement that weaknesses have been carefully addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-page introduction — summarize major changes only
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the major substantive changes that address the key weaknesses but do not attempt to list every minor edit on a one-page response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick the few things most likely to have driven the score away from the payline; minor issues should be handled in the revised text rather than the one-page summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize issues that drove the score
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and address the major issues most likely responsible for the low impact score rather than trying to address every minor critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criterion sub-scores (e.g., approach, significance) and recurring reviewer comments to identify priorities; address 3–4 major weaknesses thoroughly in the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark and document revisions in the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Denote where significant revisions occur in the revised proposal (e.g., vertical margin lines, section references) so reviewers can find changes easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common methods: vertical revision bars in the margin, clear section pointers (e.g., 'BC2.4'); avoid distracting font changes like italicizing everything; point reviewers to specific headers/sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote critique and give concrete specific responses
rubrics_metrics.description: For each specific critique addressed, reproduce the reviewer’s comment then provide a concrete response describing what was changed and where to find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain not just that you added something (e.g., statistician) but what they do, how they improve the approach, and where that is described; use the critique label (e.g., C2.4) to orient the reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add or clarify personnel roles with specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reviewer recommends additional personnel (e.g., a statistical consultant), add them and describe their exact contributions to the analysis/approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just state 'a statistician was added'; specify what they will do, how they've contributed to analysis plans, and point to the revised text that details their role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete or substantially revise aims reviewers dislike
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers uniformly dislike or find an aim unclear, consider deleting or reconceptualizing that aim rather than defending it pointlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the rationale for removing an aim and show that you thoughtfully considered alternatives; don’t simply say 'you were right'—show reasoning for the change and how it improves coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add pilot/preliminary data only when it clearly supports claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for feasibility or pilot data, include new preliminary studies that directly demonstrate feasibility and explicitly state what they show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: rushed pilot work that is unclear can amplify concerns; examine pilot data critically before adding; describe how the data addresses the specific reviewer concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address statistical power concerns thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers note missing power analyses, explain the complexities of power estimation for your methods, present chosen power approaches, and offer alternative evidence (e.g., converging effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise tutorial for reviewers if standard power formulas don't apply; specify what you did to estimate power and why it is appropriate for the analysis technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address generalizability concerns explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers question generalizability (e.g., across socioeconomic status), state analytic plans to include those variables and explain expected effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe planned models (e.g., covariates), why you expect or don’t expect effects, and how analyses will test for generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify dependent variables and measurement rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why particular dependent variables are used (e.g., accuracy vs. reaction time), when each is appropriate, and how they contribute to hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feasibility data to show detection capability and clarify measurement choices so reviewers understand why multiple DVs are needed and what each indicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch tone and avoid adversarial language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid confrontation or belittling reviewers; do not call reviewers 'stupid' or accuse them of ignorance—take responsibility where appropriate and correct misunderstandings calmly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adversarial language is self-defeating; find common ground, acknowledge lack of clarity in the original submission, and provide explanations or clarifications without hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make substantive, nontrivial revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A revision must be substantive to improve score; do not rely on trivial edits if your score was poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the revision to require substantial rewriting, new analyses or data, or reconceptualization; allocate significant time and effort similar to the initial submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple sources to shape the revision
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to reviewer comments, draw on new preliminary data, recent literature, collaborator contributions, and lab progress to inform revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate anything since the initial submission that affects feasibility, methods, or rationale; update references and integrate collaborators' new findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adding irrelevant material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not add content unrelated to reviewer concerns, since new material invites new critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be comprehensive but targeted: add only what addresses reviewers' concerns or legitimately strengthens your argument; avoid tangential expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blindly implement reviewers’ suggested methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t simply do what a reviewer suggests without thinking through feasibility and consequences; analyze the underlying concern and choose an optimal solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a suggestion (e.g., an experimental technique) is impractical or introduces problems, explain why and propose a better alternative that addresses the critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate sufficient time and perform internal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the resubmission process like a full grant; spend nontrivial time rewriting and perform internal peer review before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot rush a resubmission; solicit feedback from mentors/colleagues and iterate on the revision similarly to the initial grant writing cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: For nondiscussed proposals, interpret critiques carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that nondiscussed proposals lack a panel summary and thus have greater variability; use criterion scores and reviewer consistencies to infer priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers may have limited insight for nondiscussed grants; look for patterns across the three critiques and reconcile strengths/weaknesses with criterion sub-scores to identify likely drivers of the score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use criterion scores to target revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine sub-scores (e.g., significance, approach, investigators) to identify which domain most lowered the impact score and focus revisions there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If approach = poor, prioritize methodological clarifications or additional data; if investigator = 'good', consider ways to demonstrate stronger productivity or environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct factual errors tactfully
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviews contain provable factual mistakes, correct them without confrontation: clarify, cite the supporting parts of the proposal, and add clarifying text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point reviewers to where the information is stated in the revised text and restate necessary facts succinctly; do not attack the reviewer for the error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain trade-offs and what was removed to add material
rubrics_metrics.description: If you add information (e.g., extra methods or pilot data) at the expense of other text, explicitly state what was reduced or removed to make room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents future reviewers from criticizing omissions and shows thoughtful editorial choices: e.g., 'In order to provide X additional information, we reduced section Y.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when to reconceptualize or abandon an approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider abandoning a particular experimental approach when multiple reviewers clearly state it cannot advance the field or lack of enthusiasm is persistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive pivot is to retain the overarching question but pursue alternate approaches; consult mentors and program officer before abandoning a research theme entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address perceptions of investigator productivity and excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers rate the investigator team as merely 'good,' take steps to demonstrate excellence (publications, stronger environment) and discuss this with your program officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve demonstrable productivity where possible; use the one-page response to briefly note productivity efforts or plans to strengthen the team's record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be persuasive: sell your proposal to reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Act as a salesperson: convince reviewers of the importance of your work and be their 'best buddy'—persuasion and collegial tone matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid antagonism; focus on clear, concise arguments and evidence that elicit enthusiasm from reviewers rather than defensive rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heed direct reviewer-to-PI comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to comments given directly to the PI by a reviewer (not included in the summary) as these often contain constructive, actionable advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as gifts; incorporate suggested readings, techniques, or directions where they are appropriate and feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: For terse or inconsistent reviews, seek external feedback and reconceptualize messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviews are very terse, inconsistent, or appear to not match numeric scores, seek outside readers and focus on improving clarity and messaging rather than small fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mentors/colleagues in your field to identify likely missing details or framing problems; reconceptualization and clearer communication can overcome terse critiques.
